stops.name: Gohlis, the farmhouse where 'An die Freude' is written
stops.campa: In the summer he lodges in a plain farmhouse in the village of Gohlis outside Leipzig. Here, in the fullness of his rescued happiness and his new brotherhood with Körner, he writes the Ode An die Freude: 'Freude, schöner Götterfunken.' All men shall be brothers; joy is the spark of the gods; above the starry canopy a loving Father must dwell. It is a song of the whole human race made kin. Beethoven will one day set it thundering into the choir of the Ninth Symphony.
stops.quote: Freude, schöner Götterfunken, / Tochter aus Elysium, / Wir betreten feuertrunken, / Himmlische, dein Heiligtum! / Deine Zauber binden wieder, / Was die Mode streng geteilt; / Alle Menschen werden Brüder, / Wo dein sanfter Flügel weilt.

stops.name: Dresden and Loschwitz, Körner's vineyard, the ode completed
stops.campa: He follows Körner to Dresden and to the vineyard cottage at Loschwitz above the Elbe. Inspired by the meadows and the river, he completes An die Freude and on 29 November sends it to Göschen for the Thalia. Through these Saxon summers he also labours at Don Karlos, turning from stormy prose to the grand blank verse of his maturity, and shapes his prose Geisterseher. The years of Körner's friendship are the calm harbour that carries him toward Weimar and history.

stops.name: Weimar, arrival in the city of the Muses
stops.campa: Schiller comes to Weimar, the little residence of Duke Karl August that Goethe, Wieland, and Herder have made the capital of German letters. Goethe himself is away in Italy; Schiller is received by Wieland and Herder and by Charlotte von Kalb. He finishes Don Karlos and turns, for bread and for depth, to history, writing his Geschichte des Abfalls der vereinigten Niederlande, the revolt of the Netherlands against Spain. History will open him the door he cannot enter by verse.

stops.name: Rudolstadt, meeting the Lengefeld sisters
stops.campa: At Rudolstadt in the summer he is drawn into the Lengefeld house, and here two things enter his life: he falls in love with Charlotte von Lengefeld, his future wife; and, arranged through Frau von Lengefeld's world, he first sees Goethe in the flesh, newly returned from Italy. But that first sight is cold and distant; the great man does not warm to the fervid younger poet. Six years of respectful estrangement will pass before the true meeting.

stops.name: Jena, the inaugural lecture on Universal History
stops.campa: Through Goethe's quiet advocacy Schiller is named professor of history at Jena. On 26 May, before a crowd so great it overflows into the streets, he delivers his inaugural lecture: 'What is, and to what end do we study, universal history?' He divides the mere 'bread-scholar' from the 'philosophical mind' who reads all history as one great design of humanity's freedom. The students carry him in triumph. He is at the summit of the Enlightenment's philosophy of history.
stops.quote: Was heißt und zu welchem Ende studiert man Universalgeschichte?
stops.quote_source: Title of Schiller's Jena inaugural lecture, 26 May 1789

stops.name: Wenigenjena, marriage to Charlotte von Lengefeld
stops.campa: On 22 February, in the small church of Wenigenjena across the Saale, Schiller weds Charlotte von Lengefeld. Poor still, but happy, he has a household at last. Yet within a year a fever nearly kills him, the first mortal onset of the consumption that will hound him, and for a time his death is announced across Germany. The Danish prince Friedrich Christian and Count Schimmelmann send him a pension that saves his life and frees him for the years of Kant, of philosophy, of the great aesthetic essays.

stops.name: Ludwigsburg and Swabia, the return home, meeting Cotta
stops.campa: After eleven years an exile, the deserter dares to return to Württemberg: the old Duke's anger cooled, the poet now famous. In Ludwigsburg his first son Karl is born on 14 September. He walks again the streets of his boyhood, sees his aging parents, and meets the publisher Johann Friedrich Cotta, who will become the great house of his and Goethe's works and finance the coming journal Die Horen. It is the last time Schiller will see his native Swabia.

stops.name: Jena, the 'happy event,' the friendship begins
stops.campa: On 20 July, leaving a session of the Jena Society for Natural Research, Schiller and Goethe fall at last into talk. Goethe conjures with his pen the metamorphosis of plants, the archetypal Urpflanze rising leaf by leaf. Schiller listens, then shakes his head: 'That is no experience, that is an idea.' In that objection the two minds recognize each other. They walk to Schiller's door still speaking; the estrangement dissolves. Goethe will call it a glückliches Ereignis, a happy event. The greatest friendship in German letters is born.
stops.quote: Das ist keine Erfahrung, das ist eine Idee.
stops.quote_source: Schiller to Goethe, recounted in Goethe's 'Glückliches Ereignis' (1817)

stops.name: Jena, Schiller's garden house, Die Horen, the correspondence
stops.campa: From his garden house on the Leutra the friendship pours itself out in letters, the Briefwechsel that is itself a monument of German thought. Schiller draws Goethe back to poetry; Goethe steadies Schiller's flights. Schiller launches the journal Die Horen, financed by Cotta, and enlists Goethe, Herder, Fichte, Humboldt. He writes his own great treatise, On the Aesthetic Education of Man, and On Naive and Sentimental Poetry, measuring himself, the sentimental striver, against Goethe the naive and whole.
stops.quote: Auf immer also sind Sie der meinige.
stops.quote_source: Schiller to Goethe, letter after the friendship's beginning, 1794

stops.name: Jena/Weimar, the Xenien, the war of distichs
stops.campa: For Schiller's Musen-Almanach of 1797 the two friends forge together a shower of Xenien: sharp, anonymous elegiac distichs flung at the mediocrity of the age, the philistines and hack-critics of German letters. No one can tell which barb is Goethe's and which is Schiller's; they write as one. A furious counter-war of answering epigrams breaks over them. Having scoured the field clear with satire, they turn, by agreement, to build.

stops.name: Jena/Weimar, the Ballad Year (Balladenjahr)
stops.campa: In a few blazing months the friends make the Balladenjahr. Schiller pours out Der Taucher, Der Handschuh, Der Ring des Polykrates, Die Kraniche des Ibykus, Der Gang nach dem Eisenhammer, Ritter Toggenburg, each a small tragedy in verse. Goethe answers with Der Zauberlehrling and the Braut von Korinth. They read one another's drafts across the road between Jena and Weimar, spurring, correcting, competing. The Musen-Almanach of 1798 gathers the harvest: German poetry has never had such a year.
stops.quote: Und der Mensch versuche die Götter nicht / Und begehre nimmer und nimmer zu schauen, / Was sie gnädig bedecken mit Nacht und Grauen.

stops.name: Weimar, Wallenstein, the return to the stage
stops.campa: After ten years away from drama, Schiller gives Weimar his mightiest work: the Wallenstein trilogy, staged under Goethe's direction. Wallensteins Lager opens the Hoftheater in October 1798; Die Piccolomini follows; on 20 April 1799 Wallensteins Tod completes the vast tragedy of the imperial general who reaches for a crown and is murdered. The Thirty Years' War lives again on the boards. It is hailed at once as the greatest German drama of its age. Schiller has become the poet of the German theatre.
stops.quote: Ernst ist das Leben, heiter ist die Kunst.
